mou.label: Ecological Mission
mou.heading: Restoring Karnataka's Green Heritage
mou.desc: Dhare Foundation is working towards large-scale ecological conservation across Karnataka — encouraging plantation, biodiversity protection, groundwater recharge, and environmental restoration through cooperation between institutions, local bodies, government departments, communities, and civil society.
mou.greenRingDesc: Creating a green ecological belt in and around Bengaluru with 2 crore native saplings to restore urban biodiversity, reduce pollution, and recharge groundwater.
mou.tankDesc: Karnataka's tanks are ecological systems that support agriculture, groundwater recharge, birds, aquatic life, cattle, local communities, and surrounding vegetation. Dhare Foundation aims to support tank rejuvenation by:
mou.tank4: Creating biodiversity zones around water bodies
mou.tank5: Supporting birds, butterflies, insects, and aquatic ecosystems

whyTrees.label: The Science
whyTrees.heading: Why do we need TREES?
whyTrees.desc: Trees are not decoration — they are the foundation of life, climate, and ecological balance.
whyTrees.reason0Desc: Through photosynthesis, trees absorb carbon dioxide (CO₂) and release oxygen (O₂). A mature tree can absorb approximately 20–25 kg of CO₂ per year, reducing greenhouse gases and mitigating climate change.
whyTrees.reason1Desc: Tree leaves trap particulate matter (PM2.5, PM10), heavy metals, and pollutants like nitrogen oxides (NOx) and sulfur dioxide (SO₂). Urban trees can reduce airborne dust levels by 30–60% in dense corridors.
whyTrees.reason2Title: Temperature Regulation & Urban Heat Island Control
whyTrees.reason2Desc: Trees provide shade and cool the atmosphere through evapotranspiration, lowering surrounding temperatures by 2–8°C in urban areas and significantly reducing heat stress.
whyTrees.reason3Desc: Tree roots enhance soil infiltration capacity, allowing rainwater to percolate into aquifers. Forested areas can increase groundwater recharge by 15–40% compared to barren land.
whyTrees.reason4Desc: Leaf litter decomposes into organic matter (humus), improving soil carbon content and supporting beneficial microbes, fungi (mycorrhizae), and nutrient cycling.
whyTrees.reason5Desc: A single/group of trees can host hundreds of species of insects, birds, fungi, lichens, and microorganisms, forming the foundation of local food webs and ecological stability.
whyTrees.reason6Desc: Large forest systems influence regional rainfall through moisture recycling and atmospheric moisture transport. Forest loss is directly linked to reduced monsoon reliability.
whyTrees.reason7Desc: Green belts can reduce urban noise levels by 5–10 decibels. Exposure to trees is scientifically linked with lower cortisol (stress hormone), improved attention, and better mental health.

traditional.label: Large-Scale Greening
traditional.heading: Traditional Plantation
traditional.desc: Alongside Miyawaki forests, Dhare Foundation conducts large-scale traditional native plantation across open land, institutional campuses, roadsides, and tank bunds — covering more ground with carefully chosen native species.
traditional.whyNativeDesc: Native trees have co-evolved with local birds, insects, and soil organisms over thousands of years. They provide the right food, nesting materials, and habitat that exotic ornamental trees cannot. Native plantations create real ecological value — not just green cover.
traditional.step0Desc: Identify land type, soil condition, sunlight, and water availability.
traditional.step1Desc: Choose native species suited to the local ecology — trees that birds, butterflies, and insects rely on.
traditional.step2Desc: Dig pits, enrich soil with compost and organic matter for healthy root growth.
traditional.step3Desc: Plant saplings with correct spacing for canopy development over time.
traditional.step4Desc: Regular watering for the first two summers is critical for survival.
traditional.step5Desc: GPS-tagged sites are monitored for survival rate, growth, and long-term health.

work.heading: Why Miyawaki Forests?
work.desc: Small spaces. Dense forests. Big ecological impact. The Miyawaki method creates fast-growing, multi-layered forests using local species — bringing back lost habitats into urban and semi-urban spaces.
work.miyawakiHeading: A Living Home for Many Species
work.miyawakiDesc: A Miyawaki forest becomes a living home for many species. Dense native vegetation gives food, shade, nesting space, moisture, and protection. Over time, these forests become small biodiversity islands inside cities.
work.benefit0Desc: Tree roots loosen soil; leaf litter improves organic matter. Forests act as natural sponges.
work.benefit1Desc: Dense native forests trap dust, reduce PM2.5/PM10, lower heat and improve local microclimate.
work.benefit2Desc: Multi-layered native forests become habitats for birds, butterflies, insects, and soil life in cities.
work.crisisHeading: Why Urban Biodiversity Is in Danger
work.crisisDesc: Urban areas are becoming increasingly difficult for biodiversity to survive. When insects disappear, birds lose food. When pollinators disappear, plants suffer. When native plants vanish, the entire local food chain becomes weak.
work.crisisQuote: "Biodiversity is not decoration. It is the foundation of life."
